claim: Sleep loss increases AMPA-synaptic strength in the neocortex.
source: Sleep loss increases AMPA-synaptic strength and number in the neocortex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established finding, supported by citations in the introduction (Liu et al., 2010; Torrado Pacheco et al., 2021; Bjorness et al., 2020).

claim: Sleep loss increases AMPA-synaptic number in the neocortex.
source: Sleep loss increases AMPA-synaptic strength and number in the neocortex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior work cited in the introduction (Bjorness et al., 2020).

claim: Sleep loss increases the AMPA/NMDA EPSC ratio in frontal-cortical pyramidal neurons of layers 2-3.
source: We report an increased AMPA/NMDA EPSC ratio in frontal-cortical pyramidal neurons of layers 2–3.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Silent synapses are absent after sleep loss in frontal-cortical pyramidal neurons of layers 2-3.
source: Silent synapses are absent, decreasing the plastic potential to convert silent NMDA to active AMPA synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by failure rate analysis data in Figure 1F showing Ss/As for SD = 0.09.

claim: Sleep loss decreases the plastic potential to convert silent NMDA to active AMPA synapses.
source: Silent synapses are absent, decreasing the plastic potential to convert silent NMDA to active AMPA synapses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed absence of silent synapses after sleep deprivation.

claim: Sleep loss changes in AMPA/NMDA ratio and silent synapses are recovered by sleep.
source: These sleep loss changes are recovered by sleep.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by recovery sleep (RS) data in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: Sleep genes are enriched for synaptic shaping cellular components controlling glutamate synapse phenotype.
source: Sleep genes are enriched for synaptic shaping cellular components controlling glutamate synapse phenotype, overlap with autism risk genes, and are primarily observed in excitatory pyramidal neurons projecting intra-telencephalically.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sleep genes overlap with autism risk genes.
source: Sleep genes are enriched for synaptic shaping cellular components controlling glutamate synapse phenotype, overlap with autism risk genes, and are primarily observed in excitatory pyramidal neurons projecting intra-telencephalically.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sleep genes are primarily observed in excitatory pyramidal neurons projecting intra-telencephalically (ExIT neurons).
source: Sleep genes are enriched for synaptic shaping cellular components controlling glutamate synapse phenotype, overlap with autism risk genes, and are primarily observed in excitatory pyramidal neurons projecting intra-telencephalically.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cell-type specific differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Sleep genes are enriched with genes controlled by the transcription factor MEF2c.
source: These genes are enriched with genes controlled by the transcription factor, MEF2c, and its repressor, HDAC4.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sleep genes are enriched with genes controlled by HDAC4, a repressor of MEF2c.
source: These genes are enriched with genes controlled by the transcription factor, MEF2c, and its repressor, HDAC4.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Extensive activity-dependent LTP of cortical glutamate synapses can lead to increased synaptic strength of cortical glutamatergic synapses during waking.
source: At the cellular level, extensive activity-dependent LTP of cortical glutamate synapses can lead to a well-documented increase in synaptic strength of cortical glutamatergic synapses during waking.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work (Liu et al., 2010; Torrado Pacheco et al., 2021).

claim: Increased synaptic strength during waking is reflected by increased frequency and amplitude of glutamatergic miniature synaptic currents (mEPSC).
source: It is reflected by the increased frequency and amplitude of glutamatergic miniature synaptic currents (mEPSC) that are restored by subsequent sleep (Liu et al., 2010; Torrado Pacheco et al., 2021), consistent with the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis of sleep (SHY) (Tononi and Cirelli, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Increased frequency and amplitude of glutamatergic mEPSC during waking are restored by subsequent sleep.
source: It is reflected by the increased frequency and amplitude of glutamatergic miniature synaptic currents (mEPSC) that are restored by subsequent sleep (Liu et al., 2010; Torrado Pacheco et al., 2021), consistent with the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis of sleep (SHY) (Tononi and Cirelli, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: During waking, the number of electrophysiologically active synapses is increased.
source: Our recent findings indicate that during waking, not only are individual synapses strengthened (overall glutamate mEPSC amplitude in layer 2–3 pyramidal cells is increased by SD) but, also, the number of electro-physiologically active synapses is increased (increased frequency in correlation with unaltered or decreased probability of release) (Bjorness et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to prior work (Bjorness et al., 2020).

claim: Overall glutamate mEPSC amplitude in layer 2-3 pyramidal cells is increased by sleep deprivation.
source: Our recent findings indicate that during waking, not only are individual synapses strengthened (overall glutamate mEPSC amplitude in layer 2–3 pyramidal cells is increased by SD) but, also, the number of electro-physiologically active synapses is increased (increased frequency in correlation with unaltered or decreased probability of release) (Bjorness et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to prior work (Bjorness et al., 2020).

claim: There is a significant interaction between AMPA matched to NMDA EPSC response for each neuron and sleep condition.
source: A two-way ANOVA analysis showed a significant interaction between AMPA matched to NMDA EPSC response for each neuron, and sleep condition (F (2, 21)=7.268, p<0.004; Figure 1A, C and E; Figure 1—source data 1, tabs 1&2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the two-way ANOVA analysis of the experimental data.

claim: There is a significant difference in AMPA/NMDA ratio between sleep condition cohorts (CS, SD, and RS).
source: We observed a significant difference between sleep condition cohorts (non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test, p<0.0022).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Kruskal-Wallis test of the AMPA/NMDA ratio data.

claim: The AMPA/NMDA ratio differs significantly between control sleep (CS) and sleep deprivation (SD) conditions (p<0.031).
source: Significance tests for multiple comparisons between sleep conditions, gave CS-SD, p<0.031; SD-RS, p<0.005; and CS-RS, p<0.191 (Two-stage linear step-up procedure of Benjamini, Krieger, and Yekutieli; Figure 1—source data 1, tabs1&3; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a statistical result from multiple comparison tests of the AMPA/NMDA ratio data.

claim: The AMPA/NMDA ratio differs significantly between sleep deprivation (SD) and recovery sleep (RS) conditions (p<0.005).
source: Significance tests for multiple comparisons between sleep conditions, gave CS-SD, p<0.031; SD-RS, p<0.005; and CS-RS, p<0.191 (Two-stage linear step-up procedure of Benjamini, Krieger, and Yekutieli; Figure 1—source data 1, tabs1&3; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a statistical result from multiple comparison tests of the AMPA/NMDA ratio data.

claim: Silent synapses can convert to active, non-silent synapses by LTP-induced AMPAR insertion into the post-synaptic active zone.
source: After activation by LTP-evoking stimulation, these 'silent' synapses can convert to active, non-silent synapses by virtue of LTP-induced AMPAR insertion into the post-synaptic active zone (Liao et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citation to prior work (Liao et al., 1995).

claim: There is a significant interaction for failure rates at Vhold = -90 mV and Vhold = +50 mV, and the three sleep conditions.
source: As with the EPSC amplitude analysis, there was a significant interaction for failure rates at Vhold = –90 mv and Vhold = +50 mV, and the three sleep conditions (p<0.031; F (1.742, 8.708)=5.550; Figure 1—source data 1, Tabs 4&5; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of failure rate data.

claim: There is no significant difference between FR-90 and FR+50 in sleep deprivation (SD) condition (p<0.916), indicating far fewer numbers of silent synapses.
source: Multiple comparisons (Šídák's multiple comparisons test; Figure 1—source data 1, Tab 5) of mean FR at Vhold = –90 mv (for As) and Vhold = +50 mV (for As +Ss) across sleep conditions, revealed no significant difference between FR-90 and FR+50 in SD (p<0.916), indicating far fewer numbers of silent synapses (Ss) in this condition.
evidence: This is a statistical result from multiple comparison tests of failure rate data, with interpretation.

claim: Both control sleep (CS) and recovery sleep (RS) restore the number of silent synapses.
source: However, both CS and RS restored the number of Ss. FR-90 is significantly smaller than FR+50 for both CS and RS (p<0.030 and <0.0035, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis of failure rate data.

claim: Ss/As for control sleep (CS) = 1.44.
source: Ss/As for CS = 1.44 and for RS = 1.46, compared to SD = 0.09.
evidence: This is a calculated value from the failure rate data.

claim: Ss/As for recovery sleep (RS) = 1.46.
source: Ss/As for CS = 1.44 and for RS = 1.46, compared to SD = 0.09.
evidence: This is a calculated value from the failure rate data.

claim: Ss/As for sleep deprivation (SD) = 0.09.
source: Ss/As for CS = 1.44 and for RS = 1.46, compared to SD = 0.09.
evidence: This is a calculated value from the failure rate data.

claim: There is a significant difference for failure rate ratio (FRR) between sleep condition cohorts.
source: As with the AMPA/NMDA RR, we observed a significant difference for FRR between sleep condition cohorts (non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis test, p<0.0006).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Kruskal-Wallis test of the failure rate ratio data.

claim: The failure rate ratio differs significantly between control sleep (CS) and sleep deprivation (SD) conditions (p<0.02).
source: Significance tests for multiple comparisons between sleep conditions, gave CS-SD, p0.02; SD-RS, p<0.0012; and CS- RS, p<0.366 (Two-stage linear step-up procedure of Benjamini, Krieger, and Yekutieli; Figure 1—source data 1, tabs 4&6; Figure 1F)
evidence: This is a statistical result from multiple comparison tests of the failure rate ratio data.

claim: The failure rate ratio differs significantly between sleep deprivation (SD) and recovery sleep (RS) conditions (p<0.0012).
source: Significance tests for multiple comparisons between sleep conditions, gave CS-SD, p0.02; SD-RS, p<0.0012; and CS- RS, p<0.366 (Two-stage linear step-up procedure of Benjamini, Krieger, and Yekutieli; Figure 1—source data 1, tabs 4&6; Figure 1F)
evidence: This is a statistical result from multiple comparison tests of the failure rate ratio data.

claim: There are few if any silent synapses available for conversion by LTP to active synapses following sleep deprivation.
source: This suggests there are few if any silent synapses available for conversion by LTP to active synapses following SD and this availability is recovered by sleep.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the failure rate data showing minimal silent synapses after SD.

claim: The availability of silent synapses for conversion by LTP is recovered by sleep.
source: This suggests there are few if any silent synapses available for conversion by LTP to active synapses following SD and this availability is recovered by sleep.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the failure rate data showing recovery of silent synapses after RS.

claim: The sleep condition had no significant effect on the expression-based clustering of nuclei.
source: The sleep condition had no significant effect on the expression-based clustering nor on the distribution and numbers of nuclei per cell sub-type across sleep conditions (Figure 2C; Figure 2—source data 1, tabs 1,2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by UMAP clustering analysis shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The sleep condition had no significant effect on the distribution and numbers of nuclei per cell sub-type.
source: The sleep condition had no significant effect on the expression-based clustering nor on the distribution and numbers of nuclei per cell sub-type across sleep conditions (Figure 2C; Figure 2—source data 1, tabs 1,2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by cell distribution analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Sleep deprivation (SD) condition is associated with a significantly increased number of transcripts per nucleus across sleep condition, matched for cell subtype.
source: However, the SD condition was associated with a significantly increased number of transcripts/nucleus across sleep condition, matched for cell subtype (two-way ANOVA, UMI/Nucleus(subType) × Condition(CSvsSD), F (16, 96)=3.004, p=0.0004; Wilcoxon matched-pairs, p≤0.0001; Figure 2—source data 1, tab 3; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis of UMI counts shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In response to 6 hr of sleep deprivation, both increased and decreased gene expression was observed in all cell subtypes.
source: In response to 6 hr of SD from ZT = 0–6, both increased and decreased gene expression was observed in all cell subtypes (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by differential gene expression analysis.

claim: There is a trend for increased DEGs in cell types expressing a greater number of genes.
source: Predictably, there is a trend for increased DEGs in cell types expressing a greater number of genes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the correlation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The greatest proportion of sleep DEGs (~69%) is expressed by ExIT cell types.
source: The greatest proportion of sleep DEGs is ~69%, expressed by ExIT cell types, while the next largest proportion is ~17% for IN cell types (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the pie chart shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The next largest proportion of sleep DEGs (~17%) is expressed by IN (inhibitory neuron) cell types.
source: The greatest proportion of sleep DEGs is ~69%, expressed by ExIT cell types, while the next largest proportion is ~17% for IN cell types (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the pie chart shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Bayesian probability of sleep loss DEGs for ExIT subtype is more than threefold greater compared to any other class of cells.
source: The Bayesian probability of sleep loss DEGs, for cell subtype, is more than threefold greater for excitatory intratelencephalically projecting neurons (ExIT subtype, pyramidal cells BRAIN Initiative Cell Census Network BICCN, 2021) compared to any other class of cells (Figure 3C; Figure 3—source data 1, tabs1,2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the Bayesian probability analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ExIT class neurons comprise the major target of sleep function with respect to transcriptomic-mediated changes in the frontal cortex.
source: These observations suggest, with respect to transcriptomic-mediated changes in the frontal cortex, the ExIT class neurons comprise the major target of sleep function and extend earlier observations that frontal glutamatergic neurons are the primary targets of the SD transcriptomic response (Bjorness et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Bayesian probability analysis and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cell-type specific DEGs show class-selective enrichment of autism spectrum disorder genes (ASD).
source: We found class-selective enrichment of both autism spectrum disorder genes (ASD; Figure 4A; Figure 4—source data 1, tabs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) and synaptic shaping components (SSC; Figure 4A; Figure 4—source data 1, tabs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cell-type specific DEGs show class-selective enrichment of synaptic shaping components (SSC).
source: We found class-selective enrichment of both autism spectrum disorder genes (ASD; Figure 4A; Figure 4—source data 1, tabs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) and synaptic shaping components (SSC; Figure 4A; Figure 4—source data 1, tabs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Enrichment of sleep-responsive DEGs by SSC and ASD genes is strongest for ExIT (L 2-3, 4-5, 5) pyramidal neurons (Chi square with Yates correction p<0.006).
source: Enrichment of sleep-responsive DEGs by SSC and ASD genes, is strongest for ExIT (L 2–3, 4–5, 5) pyramidal neurons (Chi square with Yates correction p<0.006).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis of enrichment data.

source: In particular, a number of these sleep need ExIT-DEGs encode proteins that can directly affect AMPA/NMDA ratio and silent synapse numbers, including Dcc (Horn et al., 2013), Dgkb (Kakefuda et al., 2016), Gpc6 (Sato et al., 2016), Grin3a (Pérez-Otaño et al., 2016), Kif17 (Setou et al., 2000; Iwata et al., 2020), Kirrl3 (Martin et al., 2015), and Ptprf (Sclip and Südhof, 2020).

claim: The transcription factor protein MEF2c is necessary for sleep loss gene expression.
source: The transcription factor protein, MEF2c, is necessary for sleep loss gene expression (Bjorness et al., 2020).

claim: ExIT sleep loss genes are significantly enriched with MEF2c target genes (p<0.0001).

evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by statistical analysis of enrichment data and citations.

claim: Class II histone deacetylases 4/5 (HD4, HD5) are MEF2c binding partners and repressors.
source: Class II histone deacetylases 4/5 (referred hereafter as HD4, HD5) are MEF2c binding partners and repressors (McKinsey et al., 2000), that can shuttle in and out of the nucleus and are trapped in the cytoplasm when phosphorylated by SIKinases (salt-induced kinases Kim et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2022), known to become active in conditions of high sleep need.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: HD4/5 can shuttle in and out of the nucleus and are trapped in the cytoplasm when phosphorylated by SIKinases.

evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: SIKinases (salt-induced kinases) become active in conditions of high sleep need.

claim: As the mouse sleep phase progresses, HD4/5 is progressively de-phosphorylated in association with decreased sleep need.
source: As the mouse sleep phase progresses HD4/5 is progressively de-phosphorylated in association with decreased sleep need and conversely, as the mouse active phase progresses, HD4/5 is progressively phosphorylated in association with increased sleep need (see Figure 4 in Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: As the mouse active phase progresses, HD4/5 is progressively phosphorylated in association with increased sleep need.
source: As the mouse sleep phase progresses HD4/5 is progressively de-phosphorylated in association with decreased sleep need and conversely, as the mouse active phase progresses, HD4/5 is progressively phosphorylated in association with increased sleep need (see Figure 4 in Zhou et al., 2022).

claim: The sleep loss genes observed in frontal cortical ExIT neurons are enriched for DEGs in response to expression of HD4cn (p<0.0001).
